title: Rational Serre presentation theorem for a reduced root system
statement: Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $\mathbf Q$-vector space and $R\subset V\setminus\{0\}$ finite and spanning. Suppose given $c_\alpha\in V^\vee$ with $c_\alpha(\alpha)=2$, $c_\alpha(R)\subset\mathbf Z$, each $s_\alpha(v)=v-c_\alpha(v)\alpha$ permuting $R$, and $R\cap\mathbf Q\alpha=\{\alpha,-\alpha\}$. Then $R$ admits a simple-root base $\Delta=\{\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r\}$, meaning a rational basis in which every root has integer coordinates all nonnegative or all nonpositive. For any such base put $a_{ij}=c_{\alpha_i}(\alpha_j)$. Form the rational Lie algebra $\mathfrak s(A)$ with generators $H_i,E_i,F_i$ and relations $$[H_i,H_j]=0,\quad [E_i,F_j]=\delta_{ij}H_i,\quad [H_i,E_j]=a_{ij}E_j,\quad [H_i,F_j]=-a_{ij}F_j,$$ $$ (\operatorname{ad}E_i)^{1-a_{ij}}E_j=(\operatorname{ad}F_i)^{1-a_{ij}}F_j=0\quad(i\ne j).$$ Here a presentation means the quotient of the free Lie algebra by the ideal generated by these relations; Lie algebra, ideal and adjoint action are as in [def-wf-lie-algebra]. This presented algebra is finite-dimensional and semisimple [def-wf-semisimple-lie-algebra]. The $H_i$ are independent and span a maximal abelian subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ acting diagonally on $\mathfrak s(A)$. The identification $\mathfrak h\simeq V^\vee$, $H_i\mapsto c_{\alpha_i}$, identifies its nonzero adjoint weights with exactly $R$, each with one-dimensional weight space, and its coroot elements with the $c_\alpha$. For $r=0$ the presentation is the zero algebra.

source.place: Appendix C.21--C.22, printed p.612 (existence of a base); Section 23h, Theorem 23.63, first proof, printed pp.503--504, and characteristic-zero extension on p.508; the displayed Serre relations on p.504 require the sign and letter corrections recorded in report.md.

proof.text: If $R=\varnothing$, spanning gives $V=0$ and the free Lie algebra on no generators is zero, proving every assertion. Otherwise let $W$ be generated by the given $s_\alpha$. It embeds in the permutation group of $R$, since $R$ spans, so it is finite. Choose rational coordinates on $V$ and average their dot product: $B(x,y)=\sum_{w\in W}(wx)\cdot(wy)$. This is positive definite, rational and $W$-invariant. The $+1$ and $-1$ eigenspaces of $s_\alpha$ are $B$-orthogonal, whence $c_\alpha(x)=2B(x,\alpha)/B(\alpha,\alpha)$. Thus the coroots span $V^\vee$, are injectively indexed by $R$, and $c_{w\alpha}=c_\alpha\circ w^{-1}$. Indeed equality of coroots forces proportional roots, hence roots equal by the displayed formula and reducedness. Extending $B$ to $V_{\mathbf R}$ gives precisely the orthogonal-reflection hypotheses. Two rational vectors proportional over $\mathbf R$ are proportional over $\mathbf Q$ by comparing a nonzero rational coordinate; hence real reducedness also holds.

source.place: Appendix C.19–C.20, printed p.611; the averaging construction and its displayed coroot formula.

proof.text: The complement of the finitely many real root hyperplanes is nonempty: in coordinates the curve $(1,t,\ldots,t^{\dim V-1})$ lies on any specified proper hyperplane for only finitely many $t$, since its defining polynomial is nonzero. Choose $t$ outside their union and its connected component. The chamber-to-base bijection of [lem-sfb-root-chamber-simple-transitivity] supplies a real base $\Delta\subset R$. Its determinant in rational coordinates is nonzero, so it is also a rational basis; the same-sign integer expansions are unchanged. This proves existence. For the remaining argument fix ANY rational simple-root base $\Delta\subset R$, with all roots having same-sign integer coordinates. The pairing of $V$ with $V^\vee$ and the indexed families $(\alpha,c_\alpha)$ satisfy every hypothesis of [lem-sfb-root-base-rational-integral-spans]: step 1 gives coroot spanning, injectivity and simultaneous reflection permutations, and the given hypotheses give integral pairings and reducedness. That node therefore makes the simple coroots a rational basis. Consequently the map from the abstract span of the $H_i$ to $V^\vee$, $H_i\mapsto c_{\alpha_i}$, is an isomorphism.

source.place: Appendix C.21–C.22, p.612; simple coroot bases C.26, p.613.

proof.text: For $i\ne j$, the root $s_i\alpha_j=\alpha_j-a_{ij}\alpha_i$ has $\alpha_j$-coefficient $1$. The base sign condition forces its $\alpha_i$-coefficient $-a_{ij}$ to be nonnegative. The formula for $B$ gives $a_{ij}=0\iff a_{ji}=0$, while $a_{ii}=2$. Apply [lem-sfb-serre-graded-triangular-quotient] to this integer matrix. Its defining quotient is exactly the algebra in the item. Write $L_\beta$ for its graded component of degree $\beta=\sum_im_i\alpha_i$. The simple roots are independent, so distinct multidegrees remain distinct vectors. The cited decomposition gives $L_0=\bigoplus_i\mathbf QH_i$, $L_{\pm\alpha_i}=\mathbf QE_i,\mathbf QF_i$ respectively, both nonzero, no degrees of mixed sign, and no degree $n\alpha_i$ for $|n|>1$. Jacobi and the Cartan-generator relations give $[h,x]=\beta(h)x$ on $L_\beta$, first on generators and then on brackets. Step 2 identifies $h$ with $V^\vee$, so different degrees are different adjoint weights; the grading is the ordinary weight decomposition.

source.place: Theorem 23.63, first proof, p.504: triangular decomposition and Serre quotient; characteristic-zero extension p.508.

proof.text: For each $i$, $D=\operatorname{ad}E_i$ annihilates $E_i$, annihilates each $E_j$ after $1-a_{ij}$ powers, annihilates $H_j$ after two powers, annihilates $F_j$ in one power for $j\ne i$, and annihilates $F_i$ after three powers. It is locally nilpotent on every Lie word: if $D^pu=D^qv=0$, the iterated derivation identity $D^n[u,v]=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk[D^ku,D^{n-k}v]$ vanishes for $n\ge p+q$. Induction on words and then finite linear sums proves the assertion on the generated algebra. Interchanging $E,F$ gives the same for $\operatorname{ad}F_i$. Apply [lem-sfb-integrable-sl2-reflection-automorphism] with $\mathfrak t=L_0$, $h=H_i$, $e=E_i$, $f=F_i$, and $\alpha=\alpha_i$. It gives automorphisms $w_i$ carrying $L_\beta$ isomorphically to $L_{s_i\beta}$ and restricting on $L_0$ to $h\mapsto h-\alpha_i(h)H_i$.

source.place: Theorem 23.63, p.504; expanded integrability and reflection argument supplied by Q124, compatible with the rational extension on p.508.

proof.text: We now determine all nonzero degrees without assuming finite dimension. If a positive degree $\beta=\sum m_i\alpha_i$ has nonzero component and is not supported on a single simple root, then $B(\beta,\beta)=\sum m_i B(\beta,\alpha_i)>0$ yields an $i$ with $m_i>0$ and $c_{\alpha_i}(\beta)>0$. This last number is an integer. Reflection changes only the $i$-coefficient and strictly decreases the sum of coefficients. Another coefficient stays positive, so the reflected nonzero component cannot have negative sign; by step 3 it is still positive. Induction on positive integer height terminates at a degree $n\alpha_j$; step 3 forces $n=1$. Negative degrees are treated by applying the same reasoning to their negatives. Thus each nonzero degree lies in the orbit of a simple root under simple reflections and its space is one-dimensional, since the automorphisms preserve dimension. This orbit is contained in $R$. Conversely the identical height descent applies to any positive root of $R$, using its same-sign coordinates and reducedness at the terminal multiple. Hence every root is in such an orbit, and step 4 carries a nonzero simple-root vector to it. Therefore the nonzero degrees are exactly $R$, each with dimension one, and $\dim L=r+|R|$.

source.place: Theorem 23.63, p.504, expanded root-support argument; height descent uses the base sign condition of Appendix C.21.

proof.text: For $\beta=w\alpha_j\in R$, choose a word in the simple reflections provided by step 5 and the corresponding composition $\widetilde w$ of the automorphisms of step 4 (use their inverses for inverse letters). Set $e_\beta=\widetilde wE_j$, $f_\beta=\widetilde wF_j$, and $h_\beta=\widetilde wH_j$. They satisfy $[e_\beta,f_\beta]=h_\beta$ and $[h_\beta,e_\beta]=2e_\beta$, $[h_\beta,f_\beta]=-2f_\beta$. On $V^\vee$ the formula in step 4 is precisely $h\mapsto h\circ s_i$, since $s_i(v)=v-c_{\alpha_i}(v)\alpha_i$. Its composites therefore send $c_{\alpha_j}$ to $c_{w\alpha_j}$ by step 1. Thus $h_\beta=c_\beta$. As the opposite weight spaces are one-dimensional, their bracket line is exactly $\mathbf Qh_\beta$, on which $\beta$ takes value $2$ at the unique element $h_\beta$. This proves the stated coroot identification.

source.place: Theorem 23.63, pp.503–504; Appendix C.20, p.611, coroot formula; explicit normalization and equivariance calculation.

proof.text: Let $J$ be a solvable ideal. It is stable under every $\operatorname{ad}h$. Choose rational $h\in L_0$ on which the finitely many weights $\{0\}\cup R$ have distinct values, by avoiding the finite union of their difference hyperplanes. The projector onto a weight $\beta$ is the polynomial $\prod_{\gamma\ne\beta}(\operatorname{ad}h-\gamma(h))/(\beta(h)-\gamma(h))$, and preserves $J$. Hence $J$ is the sum of its weight intersections. If it contains a nonzero vector of $L_\beta$, it contains $e_\beta$, then $h_\beta=[e_\beta,f_\beta]$, and then $f_\beta$ because $[h_\beta,f_\beta]=-2f_\beta$. The span of this triple equals its own bracket span and is nonzero, so it lies in every term of the derived sequence of $J$, contradicting solvability. Thus $J\subseteq L_0$. For $h\in J$, $[h,E_i]=\alpha_i(h)E_i\in J\cap L_{\alpha_i}=0$. All $\alpha_i(h)=0$, and the base separates $V^\vee$, so $h=0$. Every solvable ideal is zero; finite dimension from step 5 and [def-wf-semisimple-lie-algebra] give semisimplicity.

source.place: Theorem 23.63, p.504; agent-supplied ideal argument proving semisimplicity directly, without invoking a Killing-form theorem.

proof.text: The grading and Cartan relations already show simultaneous rational diagonalizability of $L_0$ on $L$. Its centralizer is $L_0$: in the weight decomposition every nonzero-weight component of a vector centralizing $L_0$ vanishes, since its weight is a nonzero functional. Any abelian subalgebra containing $L_0$ lies in this centralizer, so equals $L_0$. Thus it is maximal abelian. Together with the independence from step 3, the identification from step 2, the root-space calculation in step 5, and the normalized brackets in step 6, this proves every remaining assertion of the item.

source.place: Theorem 23.63, pp.503–504: splitting Cartan algebra and prescribed root system; zero-weight centralizer calculation.
